newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: PRESS DIGEST-Australian General News - July 17.
newsitem.headline: PRESS DIGEST-Australian General News - July 17.

text.p: (Compiled for Reuters by Media Monitors)
THE AUSTRALIAN FINANCIAL REVIEW

Prime Minister John Howard indicated yesterday the Federal Government was preparing to move to a more interventionist industry policy to help economic growth and fight unemployment. Federal Cabinet's discussed the policy on Monday, which would offer investment incentives and infrastructure funding. Page 1.

Both sides of the five-week dispute at Rio Tinto's Hunter Valley No. 1 coal mine indicated yesterday they were prepared to re-open negotiations. The mining union and Rio Tinto subsidiary Coal & Allied said they were prepared to give ground in the dispute which had threatened to widen into a national strike. Page 1.

Former Labor Prime Minister Bob Hawke yesterday criticised the Australian Labor Party and the union movement for opposing the Howard Government's programme of reform for industrial relations, and argued for greater flexibility in reforming work practices. Page 5.

Heavy lobbying from the airline industry is unlikely to make the Federal Government back down on plans to penalise airlines that operate late flights to and from Sydney's Kingsford Smith Airport after the Transport Department argued strict compliance was necessary if take-offs and landings were to be effectively regimented. Page 4.
THE AUSTRALIAN

Prime Minister John Howard yesterday confirmed the Federal Government would consider a plan to give tax breaks for special free-trade zones as part of a strategy to combat Australia's unemployment problem. Howard said businesses could be exempt from taxes on imported inputs but stressed any decision would be part of a national approach to industry. Page 1.

Investigators said yesterday the bridge that collapsed at the Maccabiah Games in Israel, killing two Australian athletes, was made of planks of wood linked by wire to aluminium tubes, and did not meet Israeli building standards. Five of the most critically injured Australian competitors regained consciousness yesterday and were in a stable condition but chess player Irina Berezina-Feldman of Sydney remains unconscious. Page 1.

The babysitter of missing child Jaidyn Leskie was charged last night with the toddler's murder. Gregory Domaszewicz protested his innocence to a Melbourne Magistrates Court out-of-sessions hearing but was remanded in custody to appear before the Melbourne Magistrate's Court today. Leskie's father, Raymond, said he was waiting to be briefed by the police but had not given up hope his son would be found alive. Page 1.

The Victorian Opposition yesterday claimed the state's hospital network chiefs were the highest paid public servants in Australia, earning up to A$327,750 a year. Opposition health spokesman John Thwaites said that while the health system was in crisis and nurses and auxiliary staff were struggling to get pay increases, a new layer of bureaucracy created by the Kennett Government had resulted in a 30 percent increase in salaries for some executives. Page 3.
THE SYDNEY MORNING HERALD

WMC managing director Hugh Morgan did not absent himself from Reserve Bank board discussions concerning the sale of A$2.4 billion in gold reserves. Morgan knew of the planned sale at the time the gold mining company began a huge forward sales programme to shield it from a possible fall in gold prices but approved the push before he joined the Reserve Bank board. There was no suggestion of impropriety but the matter has raised the issue of how the Reserve Bank deals with potential conflicts of interest. Page 1.

A pregnant woman was kidnapped by two gunmen from the gates of her Fairfield house yesterday and held for 16 hours while her abductors negotiated a ransom with her partner using a mobile phone in their car. Kim Loan Nguyen and her partner Van La Duong had just returned home from the Sydney Casino where they won A$1.4 million. The kidnappers were arrested when they tried to collect the ransom money and were charged with kidnap and robbery. Page 1.

Rio Tinto mine manager Allan Davies announced yesterday the company would consider negotiating with its Hunter Valley mine workers while they remain on strike. His announcement followed a declaration by the mine union that it was ready to temporarily set side the dispute over the offer of individual contracts to workers who quit the union. Page 3.

Prime Minister John Howard told a Liberal Party meeting in Newcastle last night he was prepared to go to a double dissolution election if the Senate again rejected legislation to abolish unfair dismissal restrictions on small businesses. Howard said small business could only create jobs if it was given the appropriate climate to succeed and invest. Page 3.
THE AGE

Police charged the babysitter of 14-month-old Jaidyn Leskie with murder last night, a month after the child's disappearance. Greg Domaszewicz was charged with the crime after five hours of questioning by homicide squad detectives. Last night he was remanded in custody to appear in Melbourne Magistrates Court today. Page A1.

The meeting of Australia's police ministers in Adelaide yesterday endorsed calls for a national drug summit to tackle the heroin problem and condemned funding cuts to border patrols. The meeting vowed to urge the next ministerial council on drug strategy meeting to consider a summit involving government and drug experts. Page A1.

The Federal Government is considering reversing the direction of two decades of industry policy. Federal Cabinet considered a paper on free trade zones on Tuesday, and the main objections to the proposal are administrative, rather than philosophical. News of the possible move came as Prime Minister John Howard acknowledged job insecurity was damaging his government. Page A1.

A group formed to represent women who participated in a medical trial conducted by researchers from Melbourne University and the Royal Children's Hospital between 1959 and the mid-1970s, is seeking an independent inquiry into long term side effects of their treatment, after half the women in the group had suffered from ovarian cysts. The women were given an artificial sex hormone to stop them growing tall. Page A3.
-- Reuters Sydney Newsroom 61-2 9373-1800
